front: 40 girls (10 play chess) and 60 boys (20 play chess). Find P(chess | girl) and P(girl | chess).

back: Generally not — the denominators differ ($P(B)$ vs $P(A)$). In the chess example they are 0.25 and $\frac13$.

front: Using the chess data, are "girl" and "plays chess" independent?
back: P(chess) $= \frac{30}{100} = 0.3 \ne$ P(chess | girl) $= 0.25$, so not independent.

front: How do you read $P(A\mid B)$ from a two-way table?
back: Restrict to the row (or column) for $B$: $\dfrac{\text{count in }A\text{ and }B}{\text{total of }B}$.

front: Where do conditional probabilities appear on a tree diagram?
back: Second-stage branches are conditional on the first: e.g. the branch to $A$ after $B$ is $P(A\mid B)$.

front: 5 red, 3 blue; two taken without replacement. P(second red | first red)?
back: $\frac47$ — one red has gone, 7 balls remain.

front: Equivalent tests for independence of $A$ and $B$?
back: $P(A\cap B) = P(A)P(B)$, or $P(A\mid B) = P(A)$, or $P(A\mid B) = P(A\mid B')$.
